description: ODC (coverage of logic EDITING and REFACTORING, server and client in the same job): the lifecycle of an action that ALREADY HAS CALLERS. This job creates no action at all - it inherits everything. The base is job:logic-steps, and both target actions already exist when the first op runs: the server action WfCov_Task_Describe, which the base job declared and which is called from inside the foreach of WfCov_Project_CloseOpenTasks; and the client action SendResetPasswordEmail, which did not even come from a job - it belongs to the InsuranceApp fixture itself, written by people in ODC Studio, and is called by the ResetPasswordOnClick of the RecoverPasswordRequest screen. Both get the SAME three changes, so that the server/client contrast sits side by side: (1) add an input parameter and then remove it, (2) insert a node IN THE MIDDLE of the flow, between two nodes that were already linked to each other, and (3) rename the action. The central finding is in change (1) and is not visible in any creation job. First: when an IInputParameter is added to an action with callers, the PLATFORM creates an EMPTY IArgument by itself in each consumer node - nobody wrote that argument, it is born from the parameter, and the caller gets a field to fill in without any op having touched it. That is why removing the parameter afterwards is REFUSED by delete without force: the very argument the platform just created counts as a real consumer, and the message names it by path. Second, and this is what this job exists to show: what happens to that argument when the parameter goes away IS NOT ALWAYS THE SAME, and the job runs the control experiment with the two actions, changing one single thing between them. On the SERVER side the job writes a value inside the argument the platform created; on the CLIENT side it writes nothing. With the SAME operation - delete of the parameter with force, brokenConsumers 1 on both - the empty argument on the client side disappears with the parameter and the screen node goes back to Arguments 1, whereas the argument that was written to SURVIVES as an orphan on the server side: Arguments stays at 2, with an IArgument that points to a parameter that no longer exists. It is not an error - the module is still isValid - and the only signal in the whole model is a Warning UnusedArgument, declared in expectedMessages. The rule that remains: an empty argument is only the mirror of the parameter and dies with it; an argument with author text stops being a mirror and the platform no longer feels entitled to delete it; only a hand removes it. Change (2) shows the mandatory order of the splice - first link the OUTPUT of the new node to the successor and ONLY THEN re-point the predecessor, which is the mirror image of the AGENTS.md rule for deleting a node in the middle ('re-link the predecessor BEFORE'); the proof is not in the dump, which lists the nodes in storage order and not in flow order, but in the Target KEYS read before and after. Change (3) renames both actions with the real consumer linked and reads back what did not follow. Outside the job that declared them there are no aliases: actions are cited as 'IServerAction:Name' and 'IClientAction:Name', and a child by path, including a node's argument as 'arg:<ParameterName>'. Each change has its get BEFORE and its get AFTER.

expectedMessages.why: This is the point of change 3 on the SERVER side, not a defect. The argument that the platform created by itself in (1d) received in (1g) a value written by this job; when the parameter leaves in (3b), that argument IS NO LONGER the mirror of anything and survives as an orphan, with the text 'True' pointing to a parameter that no longer exists. The Studio does not delete it - it gives this warning, which is the ONLY thing in the model that names the damage: it says the value, it says the name of the parameter that no longer exists and it says the node. Compare with the CLIENT side, where the twin argument received NO value at all and left with the parameter without leaving a warning: in gets (7c) and (7d) the screen node goes back to Arguments 1. The difference between the two cases is a single one - whether the author wrote inside the argument or not. This job leaves the orphan on purpose, because only a hand corrects it and a job that cleaned it up would hide the lesson.

ops.name: WfCov_Task_Describe
ops._why: (0a) THE STARTING POINT IS INHERITED: the server action already exists before the first op of this job. It came from job:logic-steps; there is deliberately no logic op or spec here, because creating and editing in the same job proves no editing at all

(0b) BEFORE, the inherited server action: InputParameters 1, OutputParameters 2, Referrers 1 and the Description written by the base job. Keep the ObjectKey - it does not change in any other op of this job, not even in the rename

(0c) BEFORE, the tree: the parameter TaskId, the two outputs, and the six nodes - Start, the aggregate GetTask, the If over GetTask.List.Empty and the two Assigns of the branches, plus the End. This is the snapshot that the dump (2h) is compared against

(0d) BEFORE, who calls it: one REAL, inherited consumer, the node Describe inside the foreach EachOpen of WfCov_Project_CloseOpenTasks. This caller is what makes the rest of the job interesting - without it, adding and removing a parameter would prove nothing

(0e) BEFORE, the caller node: Arguments 1. This number is the thread of the whole change 1 - it rises to 2 in get (1d) and, contrary to what is expected, does NOT go back to 1 in get (3d). No op of this job touches this node at any moment: both times the number changes are a consequence of changing the parameter of the OTHER action

(0f) BEFORE, the caller's only argument: Value 'GetOpenOfProject.List.Current.WfCovTask.Id', written by the base job. 'arg:<ParameterName>' is the unambiguous way to cite an argument; the Parameter points to the key of the IInputParameter TaskId

(0g) BEFORE, the predecessor of the point where the new node will enter: note the Target - it is the key of the IIfNode. In get (2d) this key is a different one, and that change IS the splice. A dump does not show this: it lists the nodes in the order in which the model stores them, not in flow order

(0h) BEFORE, the successor: IncomingConnectors 1. At the end of change 2 it is still 1 - the new node ENTERS the connection that existed, it does not create a second one. The '#Type[n]' is the positional form, 1-based, and it is the only one that works for nodes with no name at all (Start, End). This If does have a name - the get shows Label 'TaskExists', which the base job gave it through the 'as' of the logic spec, and '.../TaskExists' would resolve just the same; I use the positional form here because it is the one you have to know when the node has nothing to hold on to

(0i) BEFORE, the inherited client action - and this one did not even come from a job: it is from the InsuranceApp fixture, written in ODC Studio itself (CreatedByTool ODCStudio), with the English Description that the app's authors gave it. InputParameters 1, OutputParameters 1, Referrers 1

(0j) BEFORE, the tree of the client action: the parameter CustomerEmail (type Email), the output Success, and the flow Start -> call to the server action of the same name -> Assign that reads SendResetPasswordEmail.Success -> End, plus the branch of the IExceptionHandlerNode AllExceptions that sets Success to False
(0k) BEFORE, who calls it: an IExecuteClientActionNode inside the ResetPasswordOnClick of the screen RecoverPasswordRequest. Real consumer, derived false
(0l) BEFORE, the caller node on the screen: Arguments 1. It is the same thread as (0e), now on the client side
(0m) BEFORE, the inherited argument of the screen: Value 'Email', the screen variable. This is the argument that MUST survive everything this job does - it is read back in (7e)
(0n) BEFORE, the predecessor of the splice on the client side: the Target of the Start is the key of the call to the server action. Compare with get (6d)
(0o) ANTES, o sucessor do lado client: IncomingConnectors 1, e continua 1 no fim

ops.name: WfIncludeDueDate
ops._why: (1a) CHANGE 1, SERVER - add an input parameter to an action that already has callers. The parent is not an $alias: aliases are local to the job that declares them, and the one who declared this action was the base job. The name carries the Wf prefix because the parameter is NEW (the rename further below does not, because nothing is created there)

OPTIONAL on purpose. A mandatory parameter added to an action with callers would leave the argument that the platform creates unfilled and Verify would fall on it; optional with a DefaultValue, the module stays valid without anyone touching the caller - and that is exactly the path a maintainer uses to evolve a signature without breaking whoever already calls it
the set answers 'via: SetDefaultValue' and not 'via: property': the default value is not a field, it is an ITextBasedExpression hanging from the parameter, as seen in the dump (2h)

ops.value: Se True, a legenda devolvida inclui a data limite. Parametro acrescentado por action-edit-lifecycle.json a uma action HERDADA, depois de ela ja ter chamadores.

ops._why: (1b) AFTER, the new parameter: Type Boolean, IndexInParent 1 (it enters AFTER the inherited TaskId, at the end of the sequence of inputs), the Description of this job and - note - Referrers 1 already here, before this job touches any caller. That referrer is the argument that the platform just created by itself
(1c) AFTER, the action: InputParameters 1 -> 2. Everything else equal to get (0b), including the ObjectKey and the inherited Description

(1d) THE PROOF OF THE QUESTION, first half: Arguments 1 -> 2 in a node that NO op of this job touched. Adding the parameter was the only act; the caller's argument appeared as a consequence. Note that the node's Digest changed and the ObjectKey did not: it is the same node, with one more child

(1e) and here you see what it is: the inherited argument keeps its expression, and the NEW argument comes EMPTY, with no ITextBasedExpression underneath. The platform creates the mirror of the parameter, it does not guess the value - whoever calls is left with a field to fill in, and it is only the parameter's DefaultValue that stops this from being an error
(1f) the new argument read by the parameter name: without Value, and Parameter pointing to the key of the IInputParameter created in (1a)
(1g) now an author's write on top of what the platform created: the caller now sends True. Keep this text - op (3b) shows what happens to it
(1h) DEPOIS: Value True no argumento do chamador

(2a) CHANGE 2, SERVER - a NEW node in the middle of the inherited flow. In an IAssignNode the 'name' of the create is discarded by the model: what appears in the drawing is the Label, which is set in the next op

the two inherited outputs get a known value BEFORE the If chooses the branch. Variable and Value are expressions: the set answers 'via: SetVariable' and 'via: SetValue', because underneath they are ITextBasedExpression and not text fields

(2b) THE ORDER OF THE SPLICE, first step: link the OUTPUT of the new node to the successor BEFORE cutting what existed. If the next op came first, the Target of the GetTask would no longer name the If and there would be no way to find it again without looking up the key by hand. It is the mirror image of the AGENTS.md rule for deleting a node in the middle of a flow ('re-link the predecessor BEFORE'): in a flow, the one that is re-pointed last is always the predecessor

(2c) second step: the inherited predecessor now points to the new node. The result says 'linked: Target, via: property' - the connector that already existed was RE-POINTED, a second one was not created. That is why the If keeps a single IncomingConnectors in get (2e)
(2d) AFTER, the predecessor: compare the Target with that of get (0g). It was the key of the If, and now it is the key of the new node. Connectors is still 1

(2e) AFTER, the new node: IncomingConnectors 1 (it comes from the GetTask) and Target with the key that (0g) showed on the GetTask, that is, the one of the If. The two gets side by side are the proof that the node ended up BETWEEN the two, and not beside them
(2f) AFTER, the successor: IncomingConnectors still 1, as in get (0h). The flow did not gain branches, it gained a step

(2g) the layout, which is the lane convention after touching a flow: it returns rows/columns/moved, and 'moved' says how many inherited nodes left their place to make room for the new one. Layout changes coordinates and nothing else - no link changes here

(2h) the tree, to put beside the dump (0c): the new IAssignNode with its two IAssignment, and the IInputParameter WfIncludeDueDate with the ITextBasedExpression 'False' underneath, which is the DefaultValue. ATTENTION: the position of the new node IN THIS list is not its position in the flow - the dump shows the tree, and only the parameters have an order chosen by whoever writes. What proves the flow order are gets (2d) and (2e)

(3a) CHANGE 3, SERVER - before removing, who holds the parameter: count 1, real 1, and the only one is the IArgument of the node Describe, with derived false. It is the same list as (1e) seen from the other side

(3b) THE PROOF OF THE QUESTION, second half. WITHOUT force this delete is REFUSED, with the message that names the consumer by path: "delete: refused, IInputParameter 'WfIncludeDueDate' is used by 1 consumer(s): IServerAction:WfCov_Project_CloseOpenTasks/IExecuteServerActionNode:Describe/IArgument (list them with usages, fix or remove those usages, or pass \"force\": true to break them)". The consumer that blocks is the argument that the platform ITSELF created in (1d): nobody asked for it and it still counts as a real use, which already shows that it is not an internal detail. It returns brokenConsumers 1. Do NOT read that 1 as 'an object was deleted' - read it as 'a link was broken'; what was left on the other side of the broken link is in get (3d), and it is not what is expected
(3c) AFTER, the action: InputParameters 2 -> 1, back to the number of get (0b)

(3d) AND THE SECOND SURPRISE, the one that makes the job worthwhile: Arguments is still 2. The parameter left and the argument STAYED. No symmetry at all - the delete created the argument when the parameter was born, but does not take it along when the parameter dies, because in the meantime author text came to be in there (the True of op 1g) and the platform does not throw away what the author wrote

(3e) THE ORPHAN IN WRITING: the INHERITED argument is still there with 'GetOpenOfProject.List.Current.WfCovTask.Id' intact, and beside it is a second IArgument with the ITextBasedExpression 'True' and nothing to hold on to - the parameter it mirrored no longer exists. This does NOT raise an error: the module is still isValid and the only signal is the Warning UnusedArgument declared in expectedMessages, which names the value, the missing parameter and the node. Contrast with change 3 on the CLIENT side, in (7c)/(7d)

ops.name: WfCov_Task_ReadTitle
ops._why: (4a) CHANGE 4, SERVER - rename the inherited action with the real consumer linked. The new name does NOT get a new prefix: renaming is not creating, and the name follows the convention that the action already had (WfCov_<Entity>_<Verb>). It returns consumers 1 (the foreach node) and expressionsRewritten 0 - and the zero is honest, because no inherited expression reads Describe.Title

(4b) READ BACK: the Action of the node still points to the SAME ObjectKey as get (0b) - the link is by key, the rename does not touch it -, but the node's NAME is still 'Describe'. The node's name only follows along when it was equal to the action's, and here it was the author of the base job who called it Describe

ops.value: Devolve a legenda de uma tarefa. Description REESCRITA por action-edit-lifecycle.json por cima da que o job da base tinha escrito, e depois do rename.
ops._why: (4c) a property written on a TOP-LEVEL NAMED element, which is what the data contract of this run now watches besides the entities. If this write did not settle in the model, the job would fail with 'Data property mismatch' even with a clean Verify - the contract checks what was requested against what is left inside
(4d) AFTER: new Name, new Description, and the ObjectKey EXACTLY the same as get (0b). Renaming and rewriting text create no object

ops.name: WfCov_Task_Describe
ops._why: (4e) empty list: the inherited name disappeared from the module

ops.name: WfRequestOrigin
ops._why: (5a) CHANGE 1, CLIENT - the same act in the other logic lane, and on a target that no job in this repository wrote: the client action of the fixture. The parent is cited by 'IClientAction:Name' because there is a SERVER action with the same name in the same module - the type in the reference is what breaks the tie

ops.value: De onde partiu o pedido de reposicao de palavra-passe. Parametro acrescentado por action-edit-lifecycle.json a uma client action da fixture.

ops._why: (5b) AFTER, the client action: InputParameters 1 -> 2. The English Description by the app's authors is still intact - this job has not touched it yet

(5c) THE PROOF, on the client side: Arguments 1 -> 2 in a node that is INSIDE A SCREEN and that this job did not touch. The mechanism is the same in both logic lanes - the argument is created by whoever compiles the model, not by whoever calls

(5d) the new argument on the screen: without Value, and Parameter pointing to the parameter created in (5a). THIS IS WHERE THE CONTROL EXPERIMENT BEGINS: on the server side, op (1g) wrote 'True' inside the twin argument; on this side NOBODY writes anything, and the argument stays exactly as the platform made it. It is the only difference between the two halves of the job, and it is what decides the outcome of (7d)

(6a) CHANGE 2, CLIENT - the new node in the middle of the client action's flow, between the Start and the call to the server action. I chose this point and not the one after the call on purpose: here the node has real work (to put the output at a known value before the trip to the server), and after the call it would be dead code, because the Assign that is already there writes Success over it on the next line
(6b) the output first again
(6c) and only now the predecessor. The IStartNode of a flow is re-pointed like any other node: 'linked: Target, via: property'
(6d) AFTER, the Start: compare the Target with that of get (0n) - it was the key of the call, and now it is that of the new node
(6e) AFTER, the new node: IncomingConnectors 1 and Target with the key that (0n) showed on the Start
(6f) AFTER, the call: IncomingConnectors still 1, as in get (0o)

(6g) the drawing of the client action redrawn: rows 9, columns 1, moved 8. Eight is the total number of nodes in this flow, including those of the IExceptionHandlerNode branch - that is, the layout redraws the WHOLE flow and not only the neighborhood of the node that entered. Compare with the layout (2g) of the server action, which returned columns 2 because there the If opens two real branches

(6h) the tree, beside the dump (0j): the new parameter with its DefaultValue and the new IAssignNode with its IAssignment. The AllExceptions branch stayed exactly as it was - the splice was on the happy path and only there
(7a) CHANGE 3, CLIENT - who holds the parameter before removing it: one IArgument, inside an IScreenAction. The path of the usages crosses the screen, and it is the same form as (3a)

(7b) the same delete refused without force, for the same reason, with the screen's path in the message instead of the action's path. It returns brokenConsumers 1 - the counter counts the same on both sides, which is why it is NOT what answers the job's question
(7c) AFTER: InputParameters 2 -> 1, as on the server side

(7d) THE OUTCOME OPPOSITE TO (3d), with the same operation: Arguments 2 -> 1. The twin argument left with the parameter and left no orphan on the screen - which is why the expectedMessages list of this job has ONE UnusedArgument and not two. Server and client behave the same; what changes the result is not the logic lane, it is the fact that someone wrote inside the argument. An empty argument is only the mirror of the parameter and dies with it; an argument with author text becomes an object that the platform no longer feels entitled to delete
(7e) and the INHERITED argument of the screen, with the same Value 'Email' and the same ObjectKey as get (0m). It went through the three changes without a single fix by hand

ops.name: RequestPasswordResetEmail
ops._why: (8a) CHANGE 4, CLIENT - rename the fixture's client action with the real consumer linked. No Wf prefix, and for the same reason as (4a): renaming creates nothing, and the name follows the convention of the app that already used it. It returns consumers 1 and expressionsRewritten 0, the same numbers as (4a) - and yet here an expression WAS rewritten, as the dump (9c) shows. Keep the contradiction: it is the subject of (9c)

(8b) THE DIFFERENCE FROM THE SERVER CASE, and it is worth stopping here: this get only resolves by the NEW name. The screen node came to be called RequestPasswordResetEmail by itself, and a get by the path '.../SendResetPasswordEmail' now fails with 'has no child', listing the siblings. Unlike (4b), here the node's name was EQUAL to the action's, and that is the condition: the name of a consumer node follows the rename when it was the automatic name, and stays where it was when the author gave it another. The ObjectKey is the same as get (0l) in both cases - what changes is the label, never the identity

ops.value: Inicia a reposicao de palavra-passe e devolve o codigo de verificacao. Description REESCRITA por action-edit-lifecycle.json por cima do texto ingles dos autores da fixture.
ops._why: (8c) the second write watched by the data contract, now on a top-level client action
(8d) AFTER: new name, new Description, ObjectKey equal to that of get (0i)

ops.name: SendResetPasswordEmail
ops._why: (8e) and the finding at the end: the list does NOT come back empty as in (4e). TWO things come back with the old name - the SERVER action SendResetPasswordEmail, which always had this name and which this job never touched, and the IExecuteServerActionNode that calls it from inside the body of the renamed client action. That node kept the old name with good reason: its automatic name is that of the action it CALLS, which is the server action, and that one was not renamed. Renaming resolves the homonym on one side and leaves the other standing - which is why every reference to the client action in this job needed the type in front of the name
(9a) WHAT REMAINED: the renamed server action has the SAME consumer in the usages as (0d), with the same ObjectKey. Four changes later, the call graph is the original one

(9b) the same on the client side: the screen is still linked by the SAME key as in (0k), and the only thing that changed in the usages line is the path text, which now prints the node with the new name. Same key, different label - it is the sentence that sums up the eight changes of this job

(9c) THE CALLING SCREEN IN FULL, which is the reading that closes the job: the node is now called RequestPasswordResetEmail and the expression of the If condition now says 'RequestPasswordResetEmail.Success' - both rewritten by the platform, without a fix by hand. THIS IS WHERE YOU PAY FOR TRUSTING THE COUNTER: the rename (8a) returned expressionsRewritten 0 and this expression was rewritten all the same. The counter counts consumer OBJECTS, and what consumes the action is the node, not the expression that reads the node's output; so the right number could never have been another, and that is why the proof is in this dump. The expression is also the known difference between the ODC lane and O11: there, an expression <Node>.<Output> is NOT rewritten and the module falls with ExpressionUnknownObject - with the same zero on the counter saying that all was well. The argument CustomerEmail still sends the variable Email, the IAssignNode of IsExecuting, the IMessageNode and the IDestinationNode to RecoverPasswordReset are as they were, and the new node WfInitOutcome does not appear here even once - it belongs to the body of the client action, not to the screen's flow

(9d) and the inherited public action that calls the other, which is where the two halves of the job meet: the SIX expressions that cite GetProject and GetOpenOfProject are exactly as the base job left them, the foreach has the same nodes, the aggregate keeps the two filters and the sort - editing the helper did not rewrite one line of whoever calls it. And, amid all this intact, the node Describe still has TWO IArguments: the inherited one and the orphan from op (3b), which only a hand removes. It is the last reading of the job on purpose: the damage that a signature edit leaves does not show up in the edited action, it shows up at the caller's house, and you have to go there to see it
